questions.question: For a loss outcome X=3 and retention d=5, why does the ceded payment use $(X-d)_+$ rather than X-d?
options: It makes the payment equal the full loss three.
It makes the payment zero instead of negative two.
It makes the payment equal the retention five.
It makes the retained loss negative two instead.

questions.question: At retention d, what distinguishes the stop-loss transform $\pi_X(d)=\mathbb{E}[(X-d)_+]$ from the probability $\mathbb{P}(X>d)$?
options: It is exactly the same probability with monetary units attached.
It excludes zero payments by conditioning on X>d.
It weights each excess amount as well as its probability.
It includes an arbitrary insurer loading on the mean.

questions.question: A non-negative loss X has finite mean. For finite d>=0, why is its expected excess also finite?
options: $0\le(X-d)_+\le X$ in every outcome.
Every finite retention makes X bounded.
The retention must exceed the largest loss outcome.
The probability of exceeding d must be zero.

questions.question: An analyst extends the positive-part transform to a signed cash flow $X$, equal to $-2$ or $2$ with equal probabilities. It claims $\mathbb{E}[(X-0)_+]=\mathbb{E}[X]=0$. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: Correct; positive and negative covered amounts cancel in the mean.
Incorrect; the transform is 2 because only positive outcomes are averaged.
Incorrect; the transform is -1 because only negative outcomes are covered.
Incorrect; the transform is 1; the mean identity needs non-negative losses.

questions.question: Losses and retentions are measured in euros. The right derivative $\pi_X^{\prime+}(d)=-\mathbb{P}(X>d)$ describes sensitivity to a retention change. What units does that derivative have?
options: It has squared-euro units because it differentiates a mean.
It has euro units because it is itself an expected loss.
It is dimensionless, euros divided by euros.
It has inverse-euro units because every derivative is reciprocal.

questions.question: X takes 0,4,10 with probabilities 0.2,0.5,0.3. At retention 5, what is its stop-loss transform?
A non-negative loss has tail $\mathbb{P}(X>t)=\mathrm{e}^{-2t}$ for t>=0. At retention $d=(\log2)/2$, what is $\pi_X(d)$?
The strict tail of X is 0.5 on[1,3),0.2 on[3,5), and zero from 5 onwards. At retention 1, what transform follows from those intervals?
A non-negative loss has mean 9, and its expected ceded excess at retention 5 is 6. What follows for the expected retained amount?
At retention 2, a loss has stop-loss transform 0.6 and probability 0.2 of positive payment. What is its mean excess conditional on positive payment?
For d>=0 and a retention increment h>0, what bounds the decrease $\pi_X(d)-\pi_X(d+h)$ for an integrable non-negative loss?
options: $\pi_X(d)-\pi_X(d+h)\ge h$ always.
$\pi_X(d)-\pi_X(d+h)\le0$ always.
$\pi_X(d)-\pi_X(d+h)=h$ always.
$0\le\pi_X(d)-\pi_X(d+h)\le h$.

questions.question: A proposed transform is piecewise linear and decreasing. On successive retention intervals its slopes are-0.8,-0.5,-0.2. Are these slopes compatible with the transform's convexity requirement?
options: No; convex decreasing functions need increasingly negative slopes.
No; negative slopes are incompatible with convexity.
Yes; the slopes become less negative as retention grows.
Yes; decreasing alone would permit any sequence of negative slopes.

questions.question: At a retention d with positive mass $\mathbb{P}(X=d)>0$, how do the transform’s one-sided derivatives differ?
options: The left derivative is more negative because it includes the atom.
The right derivative is more negative because it includes the atom.
They agree because the transform itself is continuous.
They differ because the expected loss becomes infinite at the atom.

questions.question: At retention 4, the transform’s left derivative is-0.6 and right derivative-0.2. What probability mass lies exactly at 4?
At retention 3, a transform has left derivative -0.6 and right derivative -0.25. What is the ground-up CDF at 3, including any mass exactly there?
X is certainly 2 and Y is 0 or 4 equally likely. Both have mean 2. At retention 3, do their transforms agree?
options: Yes; equal means make every retention transform equal.
No; X gives 0 and Y gives 1.
Yes; both give 0 because retention exceeds their common mean.
No; X gives 0 and Y gives 0.5.

questions.question: X takes 1,3,8 with probabilities 1/4,1/4,1/2; Y takes 2,8 with probabilities 1/2,1/2. Both transforms equal 5 at zero and agree at every retention d>=5. Does this partial transform agreement identify identical loss laws?
options: No; the unobserved lower-retention transforms can differ.
Yes; equal means and a common upper transform determine every loss probability.
Yes; equality above 5 gives identical right derivatives at every non-negative retention.
No; the claimed zero-retention agreement is false because the means are 4 and 5.

questions.question: A non-negative integrable loss is reported to have $\pi_X(2)=\pi_X(5)=1$. Can any loss law satisfy both reported stop-loss transform values?
options: Yes; positive excess above 5 supplies the same tail area at both retentions.
Yes; losses below 2 can have mean 1 and make both transforms equal 1.
Yes; an atom exactly at 2 can produce a positive flat transform up to 5.
No; equality at the two retentions would force both transform values to zero.

questions.question: A loss takes only $0,2,b$, where $b>2$. At retention 2 its transform has left derivative $-0.6$, right derivative $-0.2$, and value $\pi_X(2)=1$. What is the upper loss amount b?

Two claims have joint outcomes(6,6) and(0,12), each with probability 1/2. Compare expected ceded amounts under retention 10 applied once to the total versus separately to each claim. Can the total transform be replaced by the sum of individual transforms at that same retention?
options: Yes; both are 2 because total loss is 12 in each outcome.
Yes; both are 1 because only one claim exceeds 10.
No; the total-cover mean is 2 while the separate-cover sum is 1.
No; the means are 12 and 6 because retentions disappear after averaging.
